Boltz-τ: HLA–Peptide Stability from Foundational Protein Embeddings

Most approaches learn from sequence alone. We bring atomistic modelling experience and reuse rich 3D representations learned by protein foundation models.

Our leverage

Boltz-2 demonstrates the gain from transferring a pretrained structural representation. The MACE extension asks the next question: can descriptors from an atomistic-simulation foundation model improve it further?

Results by holdout

Reading the splits

A · random is the easiest: rows are shuffled. B · peptide asks the model to handle unseen peptides. C · allele holds out whole alleles. C2 · cluster is the strictest, holding out groups of similar HLA grooves. All five models are evaluated on the same ~14,500 rows spanning 75 alleles and 22 clusters.

The main pattern is simple: the sequence models are competitive on shuffled rows, then lose correlation as the holdout becomes less familiar. The frozen Boltz-2 representation degrades less sharply. Use the tabs above to check that story against Pearson, rank correlation, and error in hours.

Two caveats

C2 puts about 3 of its 22 clusters in test. Treat that column as a strong signal worth following up, not as a precise estimate of generalisation to every unseen groove.

Squeeze-and-excitation changes feature weighting, not the raw input. It starts from the direct model’s same 704 channels, learns a gate over them, then feeds either an MLP or XGBoost. It is best read as a baseline variant rather than a separate rung in a hierarchy.
